Mergers, Amalgamation, Compromise and Arrangement; Winding Up; NCLT/NCLAT; Registrar and Striking Off

iOverview

Compromise or arrangement (ss.230-232): a company, its creditors, or its members may propose a compromise or arrangement

★Must know

  1. Compromise or arrangement (ss.230-232): a company, its creditors, or its members may propose a compromise or arrangement; the NCLT directs a meeting of the creditors or class of creditors or members; the scheme must be approved by a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of the creditors, or class of creditors, or members, present and voting in person, by proxy or by postal ballot; once sanctioned by the NCLT, it is binding on all creditors/members and on the company. Notice to the Central Government, Income Tax authorities, RBI, SEBI, Registrar, stock exchanges, the Competition Commission of India and other sectoral regulators; objections by persons holding 10% or more of shareholding or having outstanding debt exceeding 5% of the total outstanding debt are permitted for the scheme.
  2. Fast-track merger (s.233): between two or more small companies, or between a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary, or other prescribed classes, with approval of the Regional Director (Central Government), without NCLT; requires the consent of 90% of the shareholders in value and 90% of the creditors in value; Registrar and Official Liquidator objections to be considered. Cross-border mergers are permitted under s.234 with prior RBI approval.
  3. Amalgamation concepts: amalgamation (merger of one or more companies into another, or of two or more companies to form a new company), absorption, reconstruction. Tax-neutral under s.2(1B) of the Income Tax Act where specified conditions are fulfilled. Competition law: the Competition Act, 2002 (ss.5-6, 20) requires notification of combinations above the prescribed thresholds; the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced the deal value threshold of Rs 2,000 crore. Take-overs of listed companies are governed by the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011: an acquirer must make an open offer on acquiring 25% or more voting rights or on acquiring control; a creeping acquisition limit of 5% per financial year for those holding between 25% and 75%.
  4. Winding up: modes - (a) by the Tribunal (compulsory); (b) voluntary winding up (now under IBC for solvent companies: s.59 IBC); (c) winding up subject to supervision of the Tribunal (omitted in 2013 Act). Grounds for winding up by the Tribunal (s.271): (a) the company is unable to pay its debts; (b) the company has by special resolution resolved that it be wound up by the Tribunal; (c) the company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality; (d) [the sick-company ground is no longer operative]; (e) on an application by the Registrar or any other person authorised by the Central Government, that the affairs of the company have been conducted in a fraudulent manner or the company was formed for fraudulent and unlawful purposes or persons concerned in the formation or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct; (f) the company has made a default in filing with the Registrar its financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years; (g) the Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company be wound up. Deemed inability to pay debts (s.271(2)): creditor to whom the company owes more than Rs 1 lakh has served a notice in writing and the company has failed to pay within three weeks.
  5. Who can petition for winding up (s.272): the company, a creditor (including contingent or prospective), a contributory, all or any of the above, the Registrar, or a person authorised by the Central Government in the case of public interest grounds; the Central Government or a State Government for the sovereignty/morality ground. Just and equitable ground examples: deadlock in a quasi-partnership (Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries, 1973: the company's formation based on mutual confidence and the exclusion of a member from management justifies winding up); loss of substratum (Re German Date Coffee Co, 1882); fraud on minority; oppression.
  6. Consequences and process: the Tribunal appoints an Official Liquidator or a company liquidator from a panel; once the winding-up order is made, there is a stay of suits against the company, restrictions on dispositions and share transfers after the order, and the Board's powers cease; the liquidator takes custody of assets, settles the list of contributories, and makes calls; the order in which debts are paid follows s.326 (overriding preferential payments): first the costs and expenses; workmen's dues and secured creditors rank pari passu; followed by employees' dues, then the Central and State Government dues; then unsecured creditors, then preference shareholders and equity shareholders. Fraudulent preference (s.328), transfers of property within one year before the commencement of winding up being void (s.329) and the offences by officers of the company in liquidation (s.339 fraudulent trading, s.340 misconduct) are tested.
  7. Insolvency vs winding up: for insolvent companies, the IBC prevails (s.238 IBC overrides inconsistent laws: Innoventive Industries; the liquidation process under Chapter III of Part II of the IBC replaces compulsory winding up for insolvency). The Companies Act winding-up regime remains for non-insolvency grounds (sovereignty, fraud, default in filing returns, etc.). Pending winding-up petitions against the company in which notice has not been served could be transferred to NCLT under the 2016 notification.
  8. NCLT and NCLAT: constituted under s.408 and s.410; NCLT has the principal bench in New Delhi and benches across India; powers include oppression and mismanagement, rectification of registers, reduction of capital, schemes of arrangement, winding up, investigation orders; the Tribunal has the powers of a civil court under the CPC (s.424) and can punish contempt. Appeals from the NCLT to the NCLAT (s.421) within 45 days (extendable by another 45 days); appeals from the NCLAT to the Supreme Court (s.423) within 60 days on any question of law. Under IBC, appeals from NCLT to NCLAT lie within 30 days extendable by 15 days (s.61), and to the Supreme Court within 45 days (s.62). The Supreme Court in Union of India v R. Gandhi (2010) held that the creation of the Tribunal is valid if the technical members have judicial competence; Madras Bar Association v UoI (2014, 2020) struck down parts of the Tribunal Rules and the 2017 Finance Act provisions on tribunal appointments Verify.
  9. Registrar of Companies and defunct companies: the ROC (s.609) maintains the register, receives documents, and may inspect the company's books (s.206). Striking off the name of a defunct company (s.248): the Registrar may strike off the name if the company has not commenced business within one year of incorporation, or has not carried on business or operations for two immediately preceding financial years and has not applied for dormant status; the company, its directors and members, and creditors can apply to the NCLT within three years for restoration (s.252); Rule: the liability of directors continues even after striking off (s.250). Shell company: a company is generally viewed as a shell if it has no active business, no significant accounting transactions or assets; the Government's 2017 crackdown led to the disqualification of roughly 3.5 lakh directors under s.164(2)(a) Verify · figures and litigation. A company can apply for dormant status (s.455) if it is inactive.
  10. Investigation (ss.210-229): the Central Government may order an investigation by the Registrar or an inspector on the report of the Registrar, on a special resolution or Tribunal order, in public interest, or by the SFIO (s.212), when the affairs of the company need to be investigated in public interest or by a special resolution. The SFIO under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs is a multi-disciplinary body that takes up serious fraud; offences under s.447 are cognizable and bailable only subject to twin conditions in s.212(6) as amended; the Supreme Court in Nikesh Tarachand Shah v UoI (2017) struck down the twin condition of PMLA s.45 (which was later restored by the 2018 amendment and upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v UoI, 2022). The SFIO's powers of arrest under s.212(8): the Director, Additional Director or Assistant Director can arrest with reasons recorded Verify.

⚖Landmark cases

Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries Ltd

1973

Just and equitable winding up for quasi-partnership companies where mutual confidence breaks down.

Union of India v R. Gandhi, President, Madras Bar Association

2010

NCLT/NCLAT constitutional if staffed with judicial competence and independence.

Innoventive Industries Ltd v ICICI Bank

2017

IBC overrides other laws (s.238); a single default triggers CIRP and the moratorium.

Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v Union of India

2022

PMLA provisions, including the twin bail conditions, upheld; a 'scheduled offence' includes ss.420, 467, 471 IPC (now BNS equivalents) Verify.

!Exam traps

  • TrapScheme of arrangement needs majority in number and three-fourths in value of the creditors or members present and voting.
  • TrapFast-track merger requires 90% consent in value of shareholders and creditors (s.233).
  • TrapNCLT to NCLAT: 45 days; NCLAT to Supreme Court: 60 days (Companies Act). Under IBC: 30 (+15) and 45 days.
